summary: Returns a table containing all rows from the specified table that are related to the current row through an active model relationship. Used inside row context (calculated columns or iterators) on the one-side of a relationship to retrieve the matching many-side rows.
whenToUse: Use RELATEDTABLE when you are on the one-side of a relationship and need to access the related many-side rows — typically inside COUNTROWS, SUMX, MAXX, or other iterators in a calculated column.

parameters.name: tableName
parameters.description: The table on the many-side of the relationship. Must have an active relationship to the current row context table.

commonTraps: RELATEDTABLE works in row context (calculated columns, SUMX rows) — it does NOT work as a standalone measure without an iterator providing row context.
RELATED traverses from many-side to one-side (returns a scalar). RELATEDTABLE traverses from one-side to many-side (returns a table). These are opposites — confusing them is a top exam trap.
RELATEDTABLE only follows ACTIVE relationships. For inactive relationships, use CALCULATETABLE with USERELATIONSHIP.
RELATEDTABLE returns an empty table (not BLANK) if there are no matching rows. Wrap with COUNTROWS to get 0 instead of an error.

examples.label: Count related orders as a calculated column
examples.explanation: Add OrderCount to DimCustomer — counts all related rows in FactOrders for each customer row.

examples.label: Total revenue per customer
examples.explanation: Sums revenue from all related FactOrders rows for each customer — SUMX iterates the related table returned by RELATEDTABLE.

examples.label: Flag high-value customers
examples.expression:
IsHighValue =
IF(
    COUNTROWS(
        FILTER(
            RELATEDTABLE(FactOrders),
            FactOrders[Revenue] > 5000
        )
    ) > 0,
    "High Value",
    "Standard"
)
examples.explanation: Marks customers who have at least one order above $5,000 by filtering the related table returned by RELATEDTABLE.

examples.label: RELATED vs RELATEDTABLE — direction comparison
examples.expression:
-- In FactOrders (many-side) — get ONE value from DimCustomer:
CustomerName = RELATED(DimCustomer[CustomerName])   -- scalar

-- In DimCustomer (one-side) — get MANY rows from FactOrders:
OrderCount = COUNTROWS(RELATEDTABLE(FactOrders))    -- table → scalar
examples.explanation: RELATED goes from many-side to one-side and returns a scalar. RELATEDTABLE goes from one-side to many-side and returns a table. Always consider which side of the relationship you are on.

sqlEquivalent: Conceptually equivalent to a correlated subquery: SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Orders.CustomerID = Customer.CustomerID — evaluated for each row of the outer table.
